title: Hatred never ceases by hatred
hookLine: a comment-section fight where every reply makes it worse, and an old rule
tomorrow: if the whole teaching fit in one verse, what would it say?

cards: A comment-section fight. Someone posts something sharp, someone answers sharper, and every reply, however clever, makes the thread longer and hotter. Nobody has ever won one of those by being angrier.
So, yesterday's question, can anger be ended by more anger? The Dhammapada answers in its fifth verse, and Pali has a line for it short enough to remember: na hi verena verani.

teach.b: Na hi: not, truly. Verena: by hatred. Verani: hatreds.
Not by hatred are hatreds ended.
In Max Müller's English the whole verse reads: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."

The verses just before it name the fuel: he insulted me, he hit me, he beat me, he robbed me. Whoever keeps turning those thoughts over, the verses say, keeps the hatred alive. The verse never says who has to stop first.
It only says how it stops. And listen for a familiar word at the end. An old rule, in Pali, is dhammo sanantano.
Dhamma again, this time meaning a law, the way things work.
You've now heard it as the teaching, as things that mind goes before, and as a rule older than any feud. That's the round: one small verse, and a week of lines underneath it.

how: Dhammapada 5 is one of the verses Theravada teachers return to when talking about anger and forgiveness, and some people learn its Pali by heart.

games.q: what does “hatred never ceases by hatred” mean?
o: an old rule: hatred ends only by non-hatred
a rule that hatred ends when both sides win
a curse on those who start the first fight

games.q: the old rule, word by word — tap the pairs.

s: Dhammapada 5 says hatred ends once the other side apologizes
it says hatred ends by non-hatred: by love, in Müller's English. it doesn't wait on the other side.
the verses before it name the thoughts that feed hatred
he insulted me, he hit me, he beat me, he robbed me: turning those over keeps hatred alive.
dhamma means the same thing in every verse
it can mean the teaching, things or states, or, here, a law: an old rule.

games.q: a friend's grandmother has died, and she asks for a Pali line from your week. which one was first spoken at a passing?
games.why: the funeral verse: impermanent, truly, are formations. in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Sakka speaks it when the Buddha passes, and its last line turns to ease.

practice: Rest one hand on your chest. Let someone you're at odds with come to mind, or, if that's too much today, just a small grudge. Say the line once, out loud, meaning it as much as you can: na hi verena verani.
Then let the hand stay where it is and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Hatred never ceases by hatred. Na hi verena verani: hatred ends by non-hatred, an old rule. Word sixteen of a little Pali.

orig.note: na hi verena verani in Devanagari letters: not by hatred are hatreds ended (Dhammapada 5).

carryVoice: Keep this one for the week: na hi verena verani, and someone has to stop first. Sixteen days of Pali.

sources.q: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 3–4 (he abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me: hatred does not cease in those who harbor such thoughts)
